title: Omniscient Tree Networks and Immortal Amoebas
gist: Nautilus's August 2026 reading list curates nine books whose common thread is anxiety about technology's grip on human agency — Jill Lepore on AI corroding democracy, Kent Anderson and Joy Moore on the internet degrading science — balanced against arguments that biology and uncertainty are still underexploited sources of innovation and hope.

insights.claim: Historian Jill Lepore argues in 'The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State' that technology has corroded democracy itself, with algorithm-driven political campaigns and corporate control of public discourse representing agency ceded to artificial intelligence.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: A mainstream Harvard historian framing AI as a constitutional threat signals that the intellectual case for platform and AI regulation is moving from tech-policy circles into general political history — watch for it as narrative cover for US platform legislation.
insights.quote: Lepore suggests that we’ve given over too much of our agency to artificial intelligence
insights.locator: The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State

insights.claim: The science-fiction novel 'Maya: Seed Takes Root' imagines a planet-wide tree network through which connected humans anticipate every action and control the world by shaping desire, with the plot turning on the one person not hooked into the network.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Fiction is converging on preference-shaping networks rather than robot takeover as the dominant AI fear — the cultural frame that eventually shapes how recommendation and attention businesses get regulated.
insights.quote: through which the humans connected to it can precinct every action, and thus control the world through the shape of desire
insights.locator: Maya: Seed Takes Root by Anand Gandhi & Zain Memon

insights.claim: Kent Anderson and Joy Moore contend in 'How the Internet Disrupted Science' that the internet has actively hurt the pursuit of science through unreliable online reports and big money skewing which questions get studied.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: A thesis that more information lowered research quality cuts against the assumption that AI-accelerated literature access improves discovery — relevant to anyone underwriting AI-for-science valuations.
insights.quote: More information is available to the average person than ever before. But how much of it can you trust?

insights.claim: Anderson and Moore argue the damage to science is reversible if the field returns to self-correcting practices, but that the window to act is closing now.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Framing reform as time-limited is the standard precursor to institutional funding and publishing-model changes — watch academic publishers' business models.
insights.quote: we can return to the self-correcting practices that make for good science—but we need to act now

insights.claim: Stuart Firestein argues in 'It Could Be Otherwise' that science should embrace uncertainty as a driver of creativity and possibility, positioning science as an agent of freedom at a moment when it is under attack on multiple fronts.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: An uncertainty-first epistemology is the counterweight to the certainty-selling posture of AI research marketing; useful as a filter on over-confident scientific claims.
insights.quote: He argues for science that embraces uncertainty, promoting creativity and possibility.
insights.locator: It Could Be Otherwise: Science in the Age of Uncertainty

themes.theme: Biology as an underpriced innovation input

insights.claim: Nicholas P. Money's 'A Is for Amoeba' recasts the amoeba as a decision-making, prey-hunting organism that has achieved a form of immortality through unusual reproduction, and argues it can advance fields from cancer treatment to robotics.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Single-cell decision-making is a live template for low-power autonomous control — a research thread worth tracking in soft robotics and oncology motility research.
insights.quote: Far from being a generic blob bumping about randomly, the titular organism emerges in this book as a creature that makes decisions, hunts its prey, and has achieved a sort of immortality
insights.locator: A Is for Amoeba: The Story of Life in a Single Cell

insights.claim: Samuel Cord Stier's 'Bioinspired' traces modern inventions back to nature — sharks informing airplane flight, ants shaping video games — and argues bioinspiration may be key to a sustainable future.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Biomimicry as a sustainability lever is a durable, low-capex R&D theme in materials and industrial design — cheaper to exploit than novel-chemistry bets.
insights.quote: From sharks helping airplanes fly to ants shaping video games
insights.locator: Bioinspired: How Nature Made Us Modern

insights.claim: Shelly Streeby's 'Science Fiction Ecologies' argues that Octavia Butler, Ursula LeGuin, and Judith Merrill built imaginary worlds directly out of the historical events around them, which is why those worlds still map onto the present.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Reading speculative fiction as encoded contemporary history is a usable technique for decoding which present-day anxieties are becoming culturally load-bearing.
insights.locator: Science Fiction Ecologies: Worldmaking with Butler, LeGuin, and Merrill

insights.claim: Kim Bo-Young's 'A Plagued Sea' uses an underwater volcanic eruption off a Korean coastal community that releases a human-transforming virus, combining geological and pandemic catastrophe in one event.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Compound-catastrophe narratives track rising public salience of correlated tail risks — the same intuition that drives demand for multi-peril catastrophe cover.
insights.locator: A Plagued Sea by Kim Bo-Young

insights.claim: 'Sacred Plants of the Americas' profiles Indigenous plant use including coca, peyote, and sweetgrass, pairing the lore with the plants' documented scientific properties.
insights.speaker: Liz Greene
insights.so_what: Continued mainstream publishing on traditional psychoactive and medicinal plants supports the cultural runway for the psychedelic-therapeutics sector.
